cor-glm-marginals.title: Canonical links reproduce weighted column totals
cor-glm-marginals.title_html: Canonical links reproduce weighted column totals
cor-glm-marginals.html: Under the canonical link, any solution 𝛃β^ of the likelihood equations satisfies ∑i=1nwixijμ^i=∑i=1nwixijyi,j=1,…,p. In particular, if the model contains an intercept, ∑iwiμ^i=∑iwiyi; and if a column of X is the indicator of a group, the fitted total over that group equals the observed total.

def-glm-deviance.title: Deviance and scaled deviance
def-glm-deviance.html:
Let 𝛍μ^ be the fitted means of a model and let θ(⋅) be as in @def-glm-variance. Assuming every yi∈M, the saturated model is the one that sets μi=yi. The deviance of the fit is 𝛍D(y,μ^)=∑i=1ndi,di=2wi[yi{θ(yi)−θ(μ^i)}−b{θ(yi)}+b{θ(μ^i)}],{#eq-glm-deviance}

and the scaled deviance is 𝛍D∗=D/ϕ=2{ℓsat−ℓ(μ^)}.

def-glm-edf.title: Exponential dispersion family
def-glm-edf.html:
Let ν be a σ-finite measure on R. A random variable Y belongs to the exponential dispersion family generated by ν if, for a dispersion ϕ>0 and a known prior weight w>0, its density with respect to ν is f(y;θ,ϕ)=exp⁡{w{yθ−b(θ)}ϕ+c(y,ϕ,w)},{#eq-glm-edf}

where θ lies in the natural parameter space Θ={θ∈R: κ(θ)=∫ewyθ/ϕec(y,ϕ,w)dν(y)<∞} and b(θ)=(ϕ/w)log⁡κ(θ) is the cumulant function, required to be the same function of θ for every admissible pair (ϕ,w). The parameter θ is the natural (or canonical) parameter.

def-glm-link.title: Canonical link
def-glm-link.html: The canonical link of a family is g=(b′)−1, so that θi=ηi: the natural parameter is the linear predictor. Equivalently, g′(μ)=1/V(μ).

def-glm-model.title: Generalized linear model
def-glm-model.html:
Let X be an n×p model matrix with rows x(i)⊤, and let w1,…,wn>0 be known prior weights. A generalized linear model consists of

  1. a random component: Y1,…,Yn are independent, and Yi has the density @eq-glm-edf with natural parameter θi, weight wi and a dispersion ϕ that is the same for all i;

  2. a linear predictor 𝛃ηi=x(i)⊤β, with 𝛈𝛃η=Xβ∈Rn;

  3. a link function g:M→R, strictly monotone and twice continuously differentiable, with g(μi)=ηi,μi=E(Yi)=b′(θi).

The inverse h=g−1 is the response function, so μi=h(ηi). The admissible set of the model is 𝛃𝛃B={β∈Rp: x(i)⊤β∈g(M) for all i}.

def-glm-residuals.title: Pearson, deviance and Anscombe residuals
def-glm-residuals.html: For a fitted generalized linear model, with di the deviance contributions of @eq-glm-deviance and hii the diagonal of the weighted hat matrix H=W^1/2X(X⊤W^X)−1X⊤W^1/2, define riP=wi(yi−μ^i)ϕ^V(μ^i),riD=sign(yi−μ^i)di/ϕ^,riA=wi{A(yi)−A(μ^i)}ϕ^A′(μ^i)V(μ^i), where A(μ)=∫μV(t)−1/3dt. The standardized versions divide by 1−hii.

def-glm-variance.title: Variance function
def-glm-variance.html: For μ∈M let θ(μ) be the inverse of b′ from @prp-glm-moments(b). The variance function of the family is V(μ)=b″(θ(μ)), so that Var(Y)=ϕwV(μ),dθdμ=1V(μ).

eq-glm-asymptotic-normality.html: 𝛃𝛃An1/2(β^n−β0) →d Np(0,I).

eq-glm-deviance.html: 𝛍D(y,μ^)=∑i=1ndi,di=2wi[yi{θ(yi)−θ(μ^i)}−b{θ(yi)}+b{θ(μ^i)}],

eq-glm-edf.html: f(y;θ,ϕ)=exp⁡{w{yθ−b(θ)}ϕ+c(y,ϕ,w)},

eq-glm-information.html: 𝛃𝛃I(β)=Cov{U(β)}=1ϕX⊤WX;

eq-glm-irls.html: 𝛃β(t+1)=(X⊤W(t)X)−1X⊤W(t)z(t),

eq-glm-joint-loglik.html: ℓ=1ϕ∑i=1nwi{yiθi−b(θi)}+∑i=1nc(yi,ϕ,wi).

eq-glm-leverage.html: qni=wib″(θi0)ϕx(i)⊤An−1x(i),i=1,…,n.

eq-glm-loglik-one.html: log⁡f(y;θ,ϕ)=w{yθ−b(θ)}ϕ+c(y,ϕ,w),

eq-glm-pearson.html: X2=∑i=1nwi(yi−μ^i)2V(μ^i),

eq-glm-phi-hat.html: ϕ^=X2n−p=1n−p∑i=1nwi(yi−μ^i)2V(μ^i).

eq-glm-quadratic-expansion.html: Λn(s)=s⊤zn−12‖s‖2+rn(s),sup‖s‖≤M|rn(s)|→0.

eq-glm-score.html: 𝛃𝛃𝛍U(β)=∂ℓ∂β=1ϕX⊤WD−1(y−μ),

eq-glm-score-canonical.html: 𝛃𝛍U(β)=1ϕX⊤diag(w)(y−μ).

eq-glm-working-response.html: zi(t)=ηi(t)+yi−μi(t)h′(ηi(t))=ηi(t)+(yi−μi(t))g′(μi(t)).

exm-glm-anodev.title: Analysis of deviance for Engel’s data
exm-glm-anodev.title_html: Analysis of deviance for Engel’s data
exm-glm-anodev.html:
Continue the gamma/log model of @exm-glm-engel, with u the centred logarithm of income and n=235. Fitting the three nested models gives

model residual df deviance change F p
1 234 39.01
1+u 233 4.27 34.73 1975.2 <10−4
1+u+u2 232 4.18 0.0918 5.22 0.023

Here ϕ is unknown, so each change is divided by ϕ^=0.01758 and referred to F(1,232), following @thm-glm-deviance(a). One qualification: the log link is not the gamma’s canonical link, so (G1) does not hold and the calibration rests not on the proof given but on @prp-glm-noncanonical, which extends the limit to this case without proving it. Income matters overwhelmingly; the quadratic term is borderline. The residual deviance 4.18 is not to be compared with χ2(232): the data are ungrouped, so @thm-glm-deviance(b) does not apply, and the small value reflects the small dispersion of the gamma fit, not a suspiciously good one.

exm-glm-binomial.title: The binomial as a family of proportions
exm-glm-binomial.title_html: The binomial as a family of proportions
exm-glm-binomial.html: Let S∼Binomial(m,μ) and let Y=S/m be the observed proportion. Its probability mass function at y=s/m is (mmy)μmy(1−μ)m(1−y)=exp⁡{m(ylog⁡μ1−μ+log⁡(1−μ))+log⁡(mmy)}. This is @eq-glm-edf with w=m, ϕ=1, θ=log⁡{μ/(1−μ)} and b(θ)=−log⁡(1−μ)=log⁡(1+eθ). Then b′(θ)=eθ/(1+eθ)=μ and b″(θ)=μ(1−μ), so @prp-glm-moments gives E(Y)=μ and Var(Y)=μ(1−μ)/m: the number of trials acts entirely through the prior weight. The dispersion is fixed at 1, so a proportion more variable than μ(1−μ)/m needs the different treatment of Chapter 38.

exm-glm-convergence.title: Two convergence rates
exm-glm-convergence.html:
Figure 34.4.1 records maxj|βj(t)−β^j| against the iteration count for the four models. The canonical-link fits reach full double precision in 5 and 4 steps, with error curves that bend downwards on the logarithmic scale: the correct digits roughly double at each step. The non-canonical fits take 5 and 7 steps, along straight lines, so their correct digits grow by a fixed amount per step.

This is what the theory predicts. Under the canonical link Fisher scoring is Newton’s method (@thm-glm-score(d)), quadratically convergent near a nondegenerate maximum. Under any other link the two information matrices differ by ϕ−1X⊤DrX, which vanishes only in expectation, so the iteration is Newton’s method with a perturbed Hessian and converges linearly — in practice, one or two extra iterations.

exm-glm-deviance-null.title: Grouped and ungrouped, simulated
exm-glm-deviance-null.html:
A logistic model with two parameters was fitted to 2000 data sets simulated from it, in two formats with the same number of Bernoulli trials over the same range of x: as 40 groups of 20 trials, and as 800 single trials. (The listing below repeats the experiment with 200 replicates, so that it runs in a few seconds.)

For the grouped data G−p=38, and the simulated deviances have mean 39.74 and standard deviation 9.43, against the χ2(38) values 38 and 76=8.72: usable. For the ungrouped data n−p=798, and the simulated deviances have mean 987.95 and standard deviation 20.62, against the χ2(798) values 798 and 39.95 — the mean off by nearly 200, the spread by a factor of two (Figure 34.5.2). Referring that deviance to χ2(n−p) would reject a correct model with overwhelming confidence.

Nothing is wrong with the sample size. The two designs carry very nearly the same Fisher information — the script checks that the standard errors of 𝛃β^ agree to within 2% — so the estimates behave alike. What fails is the reference distribution, because the saturated model in the second format has 800 parameters and grows with the data.

exm-glm-engel.title: Food expenditure: three models, two decisions
exm-glm-engel.title_html: Food expenditure: three models, two decisions
exm-glm-engel.html:
Engel’s classic budget survey records annual income and food expenditure for 235 working-class households. Food expenditure is positive, right-skewed, and visibly more variable at high incomes. Write u=log⁡(income) and fit three models with the same linear predictor β0+β1u: a normal random component with the identity link (ordinary least squares), a gamma random component with the identity link, and a gamma random component with the log link. The first two differ only in the variance function, the last two only in the link.

The identity-link fits give β^1=571.02 (normal) and 474.54 (gamma) francs per unit of log income. The gamma/log fit gives β^1=0.8629, an elasticity: a one per cent rise in income is associated with a 0.86 per cent rise in expected food expenditure. Its estimated dispersion is ϕ^=0.0177, so by @exm-glm-gamma the fitted coefficient of variation is ϕ^=0.133, the same at every income.

Figure 34.2.1 separates the two decisions. In panel (a) the identity-link mean curve is concave in income and flattens, while the log-link curve is a power law that keeps climbing; at the largest income in the sample the two fitted means differ by a factor of 1.786. Panel (b) holds the link at the identity and changes the variance function, so its bands come from the identity-link fits, the gamma one using ϕ^=0.0240 and a coefficient of variation of 0.155. The normal band has constant width and at low incomes dips below zero; the gamma band widens in proportion to the mean, as the data do.

exm-glm-gamma.title: The gamma and its constant coefficient of variation
exm-glm-gamma.title_html: The gamma and its constant coefficient of variation
exm-glm-gamma.html: Let Y have the gamma density with shape a>0 and mean μ, f(y)=(a/μ)aΓ(a)ya−1e−ay/μon (0,∞). Its logarithm is a{y(−1μ)−log⁡μ}+(a−1)log⁡y+alog⁡a−log⁡Γ(a), which is @eq-glm-edf with w=1, ϕ=1/a, θ=−1/μ and b(θ)=log⁡μ=−log⁡(−θ). Then b′(θ)=−1/θ=μ and b″(θ)=1/θ2=μ2, so Var(Y)=ϕμ2 and the coefficient of variation Var(Y)/μ=ϕ is free of the mean: the spread is proportional to the level, the defining feature of the gamma family as a regression model. With μ=4 and ϕ=0.4 the formula gives Var(Y)=6.400, and by @prp-glm-moments(c) the third cumulant is ϕ2b‴(θ)=2ϕ2μ3=20.480; both agree with the exact gamma moments in the listing below.

exm-glm-hauck-donner.title: The Hauck–Donner effect
exm-glm-hauck-donner.html:
Two groups of 40 trials, with 20 successes in group A and sB in group B, fitted by a logistic model with an intercept and a group indicator. The coefficient is the log odds ratio β^1=log⁡{sB/(40−sB)}, with standard error {1/20+1/20+1/sB+1/(40−sB)}1/2. As sB rises from 21 to 39 the evidence against equality strengthens monotonically and the likelihood ratio statistic records it, climbing to 27.301. The Wald statistic does not: it rises to 13.842 at sB=38 and then falls to 11.924 at sB=39, though the fitted log odds ratio has grown to 3.664. The standard error grows faster than the coefficient.

At complete separation, sB=40, coefficient and standard error are both infinite and the Wald statistic is 0: the test accepts the null precisely where the data support it most strongly (Figure 34.5.1). The effect occurs whenever the log-likelihood is far from quadratic over the range where the estimate lies.

exm-glm-identity-poisson.title: An identity link close to its boundary
exm-glm-identity-poisson.title_html: An identity link close to its boundary
exm-glm-identity-poisson.html: Eight counts were simulated from a Poisson model with mean 12−1.2x at x=1,…,8. An identity-link Poisson fit recovers the declining mean, and every fitted value is positive — but the fitted line reaches zero at x=9.89, barely outside the range of the data. Predicting at x=10 would return a negative mean, and a slightly different sample would push the boundary inside the observed range, where the likelihood is −∞. The log link has no such boundary.

exm-glm-marginals.title: Fitted votes by party identification
exm-glm-marginals.html:
The 1996 American National Election Studies subset records, for 944 respondents, a reported vote (coded 1 for Dole), a party-identification score from 0 (strong Democrat) to 6 (strong Republican), and age. Fit a logistic model with one indicator column per party-identification level and age (in decades, centred at 45) as an eighth column. The age coefficient is 0.1044 with standard error 0.0730.

By @cor-glm-marginals the fitted probabilities must add up, within each of the seven party-identification groups, to the observed number of Dole voters — though age is in the model and varies within every group. Among the 200 strong Democrats, 3 reported voting for Dole and the fitted probabilities sum to 3 exactly; among the 175 strong Republicans observed and fitted totals are both 167. The eighth column gives ∑iageiyi=∑iageiμ^i=121.3000.

A probit refit destroys the identity: the group totals are then wrong by up to 0.0966 and the age total by 0.6245. The discrepancies are small, because the fits are similar, but nothing forces them to be zero. The same contrast holds for the information, which under the logit link agrees with the expected information to machine precision and under the probit link differs by a relative 0.0056.

exm-glm-negbin.title: The negative binomial with known shape
exm-glm-negbin.title_html: The negative binomial with known shape
exm-glm-negbin.html:
Let Pr(Y=y)=Γ(y+k)Γ(k)y!πy(1−π)k, y=0,1,2,…, for a fixed k>0. Writing θ=log⁡π puts this in the form @eq-glm-edf with w=1, ϕ=1 and b(θ)=−klog⁡(1−eθ), so that μ=b′(θ)=kπ1−π,b″(θ)=kπ(1−π)2=μ(1+μk) after substituting π=μ/(μ+k). With k=2 and μ=3 this gives Var(Y)=7.500, against 3 for a Poisson variable with the same mean.

The caveat is essential: this is an exponential dispersion family only for fixed k. The shape enters the variance function, not the dispersion, so it cannot be divided out, and letting k vary leaves the form @eq-glm-edf. Estimating k is outside this chapter’s machinery; Chapter 37 takes it up.

exm-glm-no-maximum.title: Two ways the maximum fails to exist
exm-glm-no-maximum.title_html: Two ways the maximum fails to exist
exm-glm-no-maximum.html:
All counts zero. For a Poisson log-linear model with an intercept, if every yi=0 then 𝛃𝛃ℓ(β)=−∑iex(i)⊤β, which increases to its supremum 0 as β0→−∞ and is never attained.

Separated binary data. If there is a vector v with x(i)⊤v>0 whenever yi=1 and x(i)⊤v<0 whenever yi=0, then along the ray tv every fitted probability moves towards the observed response, so ℓ increases without reaching a maximum. Chapter 35 proves that this is the only way the binary maximum likelihood estimate can fail to exist (@thm-bin-separation).

exm-glm-residual-shapes.title: Which residual is closest to normal
exm-glm-residual-shapes.title_html: Which residual is closest to normal
exm-glm-residual-shapes.html: Two thousand observations were simulated from a Poisson log-linear model with fitted means between about 1 and 6, and the model refitted. Figure 34.5.3 shows normal quantile plots of the three residual types. The Pearson residuals are visibly right-skewed, with sample skewness 0.618 — the skewness μ−1/2 of @exr-glm-skewness, averaged over the fitted means. The deviance residuals have skewness −0.010 and the Anscombe residuals −0.081; both are far closer to normal, and neither is uniformly better. Discreteness remains visible in all three as short horizontal runs. The leverages sum to 2 (@prp-proj-leverage(b)) and the largest is 0.0029.

exm-glm-separation-irls.title: What separation looks like from inside the algorithm
exm-glm-separation-irls.title_html: What separation looks like from inside the algorithm
exm-glm-separation-irls.html:
Ten binary responses were generated with yi=1 exactly when xi>0, so the data are completely separated. Running the solver on them gives

step β^1 deviance largest working weight
1 1.36 4.589 0.245
4 5.74 0.931 0.159
7 16.95 0.0574 0.0142
8 — — —

At the eighth step every fitted probability has reached 0 or 1 in double precision, so V(μ^i)=0, the working weights are 0/0, and the iteration returns nothing. The slope was never going to settle: the supremum of the likelihood is approached only as β1→∞. Chapter 35 characterizes exactly when this happens and what to do about it (@thm-bin-separation).

exr-glm-admissible.title: A1
exr-glm-admissible.html: Describe the admissible set B of @def-glm-model for (a) a Poisson model with the identity link, (b) a binomial model with the identity link, (c) a gamma model with the log link. Which of the three is all of Rp?

exr-glm-anscombe-poisson.title: B3
exr-glm-anscombe-poisson.html: Derive the Anscombe residual for the Poisson family from A(μ)=∫μt−1/3dt, and check that the standardizing denominator is μ^1/6. Explain why A is not the variance-stabilizing transformation 2μ of @cor-tr-classical, and what each one is optimizing.

exr-glm-canonical-characterization.title: B2
exr-glm-canonical-characterization.html: Show that the observed information equals the expected information identically in y if and only if the link is canonical (up to an affine change of η). Assume that no row of X is zero, an observation with x(i)=0 carrying no information about 𝛃β. Use @thm-glm-score(c).

exr-glm-cloglog-range.title: B3
exr-glm-cloglog-range.html: The complementary log–log link for a binomial response is g(μ)=log⁡{−log⁡(1−μ)}. Show that it is a bijection from (0,1) onto R, compute dμ/dη, and show that it is not symmetric: g(μ)≠−g(1−μ), unlike the logit and probit links. Which tail does it approach more slowly?

exr-glm-concavity-links.title: C1
exr-glm-concavity-links.html: For a binary response, 𝛃ℓ(β)=∑i{yilog⁡h(ηi)+(1−yi)log⁡(1−h(ηi))}. Show that ℓ is concave for every design and every data set if and only if log⁡h and log⁡(1−h) are both concave functions of η. Verify that the logit link satisfies this, and that h(η)=Φ(η) does too, using the fact that the standard normal density is log-concave.

exr-glm-deviance-normal.title: A1
exr-glm-deviance-normal.html: Verify the normal and Poisson rows of the deviance table from @eq-glm-deviance. For the Poisson, show that if the model has an intercept then ∑i(yi−μ^i)=0 by @cor-glm-marginals, so the deviance reduces to 2∑iyilog⁡(yi/μ^i).

exr-glm-deviance-not-fit.title: C1
exr-glm-deviance-not-fit.html: Extend @thm-glm-deviance(c) to a Poisson log-linear model in which every yi is 0 or 1: show that the deviance is again a function of 𝛃β^ alone. Then show that the argument breaks down as soon as some yi≥2, and explain in words what extra information the larger counts supply. (This is the reason the deviance is a serviceable goodness-of-fit statistic for Poisson data with large means and a useless one for sparse counts.)

exr-glm-df.title: A2
exr-glm-df.html: A binomial model is fitted to 60 groups with 4 parameters, and the residual deviance is 71.2 on 56 degrees of freedom. When is comparing it with χ2(56) legitimate, and what would you need to know about the data first?

exr-glm-invgauss.title: B1
exr-glm-invgauss.html: Verify the inverse Gaussian row of the table: starting from f(y)=(2πσ2y3)−1/2exp⁡{−(y−μ)22σ2μ2y}on (0,∞), put it in the form @eq-glm-edf and confirm V(μ)=μ3. What is Θ, and what happens at θ=0?

exr-glm-irls-monotone.title: C1
exr-glm-irls-monotone.html: Show that under the canonical link, Fisher scoring is Newton’s method applied to a strictly concave function, and deduce that when the maximum exists, the iteration converges to it from any starting point at which the step is well defined provided the step is damped: for each t there is st∈(0,1] with 𝛃𝛃ℓ(β(t)+std(t))>ℓ(β(t)), where d(t) is the Newton direction. Why does the undamped step not carry the same guarantee? (Compare @prp-res-irls, where the undamped step is monotone, because the argument there is majorization rather than Newton.)

exr-glm-irls-offset.title: B2
exr-glm-irls-offset.html: Modify @eq-glm-irls for a model with an offset 𝛃ηi=oi+x(i)⊤β, as in @exr-glm-offset. Show that the working response becomes zi=ηi−oi+(yi−μi)g′(μi) and nothing else changes.

exr-glm-link-vs-transform.title: B1
exr-glm-link-vs-transform.html: Let Y be positive with E(Y)=μ and Var(Y)=ϕμ2, as in the gamma family. Using a second-order Taylor expansion of log⁡Y about μ, show that E(log⁡Y)≈log⁡μ−ϕ/2. Deduce that a least squares regression of log⁡yi on X and a gamma/log generalized linear model estimate intercepts that differ by approximately ϕ/2, while their slopes agree to this order. For the fit of @exm-glm-engel, how large is the discrepancy?

exr-glm-logistic-equations.title: B1
exr-glm-logistic-equations.html: For grouped binomial data with yi=si/mi, the logit link and wi=mi, write the likelihood equations in terms of the observed successes si. Show that the working weight is Wii=miμi(1−μi) and that the information is X⊤diag{miμi(1−μi)}X. Where have you seen that matrix before?

exr-glm-not-edf.title: C1
exr-glm-not-edf.html: Show that the uniform family on (0,ϑ) is not an exponential dispersion family for any choice of ν, and that the Cauchy family with median ϑ is not either. Which hypothesis of @def-glm-edf fails in each case?

exr-glm-offset.title: C2
exr-glm-offset.html: An offset is a known column added to the linear predictor with coefficient fixed at 1: 𝛃ηi=oi+x(i)⊤β. Show that @thm-glm-score holds verbatim with ηi redefined this way, that @cor-glm-marginals is unchanged, and that the offset does not appear among the columns whose totals are reproduced. Where would such a term come from in a Poisson model for rates? (Chapter 37 answers this with @prp-cnt-offsets.)

exr-glm-one-step.title: B1
exr-glm-one-step.html: Take grouped binomial data with all 0<si<mi and start the iteration at μi(0)=si/mi. Show that the first working response is the empirical logit log⁡{si/(mi−si)} and the first working weight is si(mi−si)/mi. Compare with @exr-tr-empirical-logit.

exr-glm-phi-moment.title: B2
exr-glm-phi-moment.html: Show that E{wi(Yi−μi)2/V(μi)}=ϕ exactly, for every observation in an exponential dispersion family. Deduce that X2/n is unbiased for ϕ when the true means are used, and explain why X2/(n−p) is only approximately unbiased when they are estimated.

exr-glm-poisson-edf.title: A1
exr-glm-poisson-edf.html: Write the Poisson probability mass function in the form @eq-glm-edf, identify θ, b, ϕ, w and c, and verify E(Y)=Var(Y)=μ using @prp-glm-moments. What is Θ?

exr-glm-poisson-equations.title: A1
exr-glm-poisson-equations.html: Write the likelihood equations for a Poisson log-linear model with an intercept. Show that they are 𝛍X⊤(y−μ)=0, that ∑iμ^i=∑iyi, and that for the intercept-only model μ^i=y¯. (This is @exr-lm-poisson-score, now a special case of @cor-glm-marginals.)

exr-glm-pseudo-r2.title: B4
exr-glm-pseudo-r2.html: Two summaries of predictive power for a generalized linear model are the sample correlation between y and 𝛍μ^, and the likelihood-based RL2=(ℓM−ℓ0)/(ℓsat−ℓ0), where ℓ0, ℓM and ℓsat are the maximized log-likelihoods of the intercept-only model, the fitted model and the saturated model. Show that for a family with ϕ=1 the second is (D0−D)/D0, with D0 the null deviance, and deduce that it lies in [0,1] and never decreases when a term is added. Why does that last property make it a poor basis for choosing a model?

exr-glm-skewness.title: B3
exr-glm-skewness.html: Use @prp-glm-moments(c) to show that the skewness of Y is γ1=ϕ/wV′(μ)/V(μ). Evaluate it for the Poisson, the gamma and the binomial, and say in each case how the skewness behaves as the mean moves.

exr-glm-sqrt-link.title: B2
exr-glm-sqrt-link.html: A Poisson model is sometimes fitted with the square-root link g(μ)=μ, because @thm-tr-variance-stabilizing makes Y approximately variance-stabilized. Find B for this link, find dμ/dη, and explain why the link being variance-stabilizing for Y is irrelevant to whether it is a good link.

exr-glm-tweedie.title: C2
exr-glm-tweedie.html: Suppose V(μ)=μξ on (0,∞) for some ξ∉{1,2}. Carry out @exr-glm-variance-determines to find θ(μ) and b(θ), and check that ξ=0 and ξ=3 reproduce the normal and inverse Gaussian rows. For 1<ξ<2 the family is the distribution of a Poisson number of independent gamma variables, with positive probability at 0 and a continuous part on (0,∞) (Jørgensen 1987); confirm from the general formula that its mean space is (0,∞).

exr-glm-variance-determines.title: B2
exr-glm-variance-determines.html: Show that the variance function determines the family: if V is given on an interval M, then θ(μ)=∫μdt/V(t) and b(θ(μ))=∫μtdt/V(t), each up to constants that only relocate the density. Carry this out for V(μ)=μ(1−μ) on (0,1) and recover the binomial row.

exr-glm-wald-invariance.title: B1
exr-glm-wald-invariance.html: Let β^ have asymptotic standard error s. Compute the Wald statistic for H0:β=0 and, using the delta method, the Wald statistic for the equivalent hypothesis H0:eβ=1. Show that their ratio is {(eβ^−1)/β^}2e−2β^, and evaluate it at β^=1 and β^=3. Why is the likelihood ratio statistic unaffected?

exr-glm-working-variance.title: A1
exr-glm-working-variance.html: Verify the approximation Var(zi)≈ϕ/Wii stated in the key-idea box, and explain which two approximations are being made.

lem-glm-convex.title: The natural parameter space and the cumulant function
lem-glm-convex.title_html: The natural parameter space and the cumulant function
lem-glm-convex.html: Θ is a convex subset of R, and b is convex on Θ. If Y is not degenerate under some θ0∈Θ, then b is strictly convex on Θ.

prp-glm-deviance-positive.title: The deviance is nonnegative
prp-glm-deviance-positive.html: Every di≥0, with di=0 if and only if μ^i=yi. Consequently D≥0, with equality only for the saturated fit, and D decreases when a model is enlarged.

prp-glm-moments.title: Mean, variance and cumulants
prp-glm-moments.html:
Let Y have density @eq-glm-edf with θ in the interior of Θ. Then Y has moments of all orders, and

  1. μ:=E(Y)=b′(θ) and Var(Y)=ϕwb″(θ);

  2. the map θ↦b′(θ) is strictly increasing, hence a bijection from the interior of Θ onto an open interval M, the mean space;

  3. the cumulant generating function of Y is K(t)=log⁡EetY=wϕ{b(θ+tϕ/w)−b(θ)} for small |t|, so the rth cumulant of Y is (ϕ/w)r−1b(r)(θ).

prp-glm-noncanonical.title: Non-canonical links
prp-glm-noncanonical.html: Let the link be any twice continuously differentiable g with g′≠0 on M, and put An=ϕ−1X⊤WX with W the working weights of @thm-glm-score evaluated at 𝛃β0. Then every conclusion of @thm-glm-asymptotics — existence with probability tending to one, consistency, the limit @eq-glm-asymptotic-normality, the plug-in version and the Wald intervals — continues to hold, as do @prp-glm-three-tests and @thm-glm-deviance(a),(b) below, which use the theorem only through the quadratic expansion @eq-glm-quadratic-expansion. The conditions are those of Fahrmeir and Kaufmann (1985): the divergence condition λmin(An)→∞, and a continuity condition asking that 𝛃𝛃𝛃An(β0)−1/2An(β)An(β0)−1/2→I uniformly over 𝛃β in neighbourhoods of 𝛃β0 that shrink in the information metric. The two together play the part of (G2)–(G4).

prp-glm-three-tests.title: The three statistics
prp-glm-three-tests.html: Define 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃Wald=(Λ⊤β^)⊤(Λ⊤A^n−1Λ)−1Λ⊤β^,Score=U(β~)⊤In(β~)−1U(β~),LR=2{ℓ(β^)−ℓ(β~)}. Under (G1)–(G4) and the reduced model, each of the three converges in distribution to χ2(q), and any two of them differ by op(1). For a single coefficient (q=1, Λ=ej) the Wald statistic is β^j2/[A^n−1]jj, the square of the “estimate over standard error” ratio that every program prints.

thm-glm-asymptotics.title: Consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimate
thm-glm-asymptotics.title_html: Consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimate
thm-glm-asymptotics.html:
Under (G1)–(G4), with probability tending to one the likelihood equations have a solution 𝛃β^n; it is the unique maximizer of ℓ, it is consistent for 𝛃β0, and 𝛃𝛃An1/2(β^n−β0) →d Np(0,I).{#eq-glm-asymptotic-normality}

The same holds with An replaced by 𝛃A^n=In(β^n). Consequently, for a fixed 𝛌λ≠0, 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛌λ⊤β^n−λ⊤β0(λ⊤A^n−1λ)1/2 →d N(0,1), and 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛌λ⊤β^n±z1−α/2(λ⊤A^n−1λ)1/2 is an interval with asymptotic coverage 1−α.

thm-glm-concave.title: The canonical-link log-likelihood is concave
thm-glm-concave.html: Under the canonical link, 𝛃ℓ(β) is concave on the convex set B. If in addition rank(X)=p and V(μi)>0 for all i, then ℓ is strictly concave, so it has at most one stationary point, and any stationary point is the unique global maximizer.

thm-glm-deviance.title: Distribution theory for the deviance
thm-glm-deviance.html:
Assume (G1)–(G4).

  1. (Nested models.) Let C(X0)⊆C(X) with rank(X)−rank(X0)=q. Under the reduced model, D0−Dϕ →d χ2(q), where D0 and D are the deviances of the two fits. When ϕ is unknown it is replaced by an estimate, and the ratio {(D0−D)/q}/ϕ^ is referred to F(q,n−p), by analogy with @thm-glh-f-test.

  2. (Grouped data.) Suppose the data consist of G groups, G and p fixed, with yi an average of wi=mi observations and mi→∞ for every i. Then under the fitted model D/ϕ→χ2(G−p) and X2/ϕ→χ2(G−p), so both are goodness-of-fit statistics.

  3. (Ungrouped data.) If the number of groups grows with the sample size, (b) does not apply and the limit is generally not χ2(n−p). For binary responses with the canonical link the failure is total: D is a function of 𝛃β^ alone, so it carries no information about fit beyond what 𝛃β^ already contains.

thm-glm-irls.title: Fisher scoring is iteratively reweighted least squares
thm-glm-irls.title_html: Fisher scoring is iteratively reweighted least squares
thm-glm-irls.html:
Let 𝛃β(t) be in the interior of B with X⊤W(t)X nonsingular, where W(t) is the working-weight matrix of @thm-glm-score evaluated at 𝛃β(t). Define the working response zi(t)=ηi(t)+yi−μi(t)h′(ηi(t))=ηi(t)+(yi−μi(t))g′(μi(t)).{#eq-glm-working-response}

Then the Fisher scoring step 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃β(t+1)=β(t)+I(β(t))−1U(β(t)) is exactly the weighted least squares estimate 𝛃β(t+1)=(X⊤W(t)X)−1X⊤W(t)z(t),{#eq-glm-irls}

that is, the regression of the working response z(t) on X with weights W(t). The dispersion ϕ cancels and never enters the iteration.

thm-glm-score.title: The likelihood equations and the information
thm-glm-score.title_html: The likelihood equations and the information
thm-glm-score.html:
Define the diagonal matrices W=diag{wih′(ηi)2V(μi)},D=diag{h′(ηi)}. Then, with 𝛃ℓ(β) the log-likelihood of @eq-glm-joint-loglik:

  1. the score is 𝛃𝛃𝛍U(β)=∂ℓ∂β=1ϕX⊤WD−1(y−μ),{#eq-glm-score}

    so the likelihood equations are ∑ixijwih′(ηi){yi−μi}/V(μi)=0 for j=1,…,p, and they do not involve ϕ;

  2. EU=0 and the expected (Fisher) information is 𝛃𝛃I(β)=Cov{U(β)}=1ϕX⊤WX;{#eq-glm-information}

  3. writing a(η)=h′(η)/V{h(η)}, the observed information is 𝛃𝛃−∂2ℓ∂β∂β⊤=1ϕX⊤(W−Dr)X, where Dr=diag{wi(yi−μi)a′(ηi)};

  4. under the canonical link Dr=0, so the observed and expected information coincide, W=diag{wiV(μi)}, and @eq-glm-score becomes 𝛃𝛍U(β)=1ϕX⊤diag(w)(y−μ).{#eq-glm-score-canonical}
